identification.summary: Spandex Tempest is Microsoft's name for the financially motivated cybercrime actor that Proofpoint tracks as TA505 and CrowdStrike as MONTY SPIDER [S1]. Proofpoint describes TA505 as responsible for some of the largest malicious spam campaigns it has observed, distributing Dridex, Locky, Jaff, The Trick and other malware at high volume [S2][S3]. From 2018 the group moved from mass spam toward more targeted campaigns using remote access trojans such as FlawedAmmyy, FlawedGrace and ServHelper against financial and retail organizations [S3][S4][S6]. By 2019 it was deploying Clop ransomware inside victim networks and ran a leak site for stolen data from non-paying victims [S7].
identification.firstObserved: Proofpoint has tracked TA505 since at least 2014 [S2]; CERT-FR dates the intrusion set to at least 2014 and notes it was first mentioned publicly in 2017 [S10].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Spandex Tempest (formerly CHIMBORAZO in Microsoft reporting; Microsoft Security Intelligence also used Dudear for TA505 activity) [S1][S8][S9]. Microsoft's mapping lists only MONTY SPIDER and TA505 as other names [S1]; other record aliases (GRACEFUL SPIDER, GOLD TAHOE, Hive0065, SectorJ04, ATK103) come from the imported MISP/MITRE records and were not re-verified here. Microsoft tracks Lace Tempest (DEV-0950), the Clop affiliate behind 2023 PaperCut exploitation, as a separate actor whose activity overlaps FIN11 and TA505 [S1][S13]. Mandiant tracks FIN11 separately as a group split out from the broader TA505 umbrella [S11].

attribution.sponsor: No state sponsor; financially motivated cybercrime per Microsoft's categorization [S1]. Microsoft's October 2020 Zerologon warning was reported as describing a Russian cybercrime group [S9].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft categorizes Spandex Tempest as financially motivated [S1]. Russian origin rests on press characterization of Microsoft reporting [S9]; no government attribution of TA505 to a specific state or named individuals was found in sources gathered.
attribution.basis: Microsoft threat actor naming mapping [S1]; Microsoft Security Intelligence posts as reported in the press [S8][S9]; Proofpoint, Trend Micro, Fox-IT/NCC Group and CERT-FR vendor and agency reporting [S2][S3][S4][S5][S6][S7][S10].

objectives: Financial gain: banking-credential theft (Dridex), ransomware (Locky, then Clop) and data-theft extortion of non-paying victims [S1][S2][S7].

regions: Greece, Singapore, UAE, Georgia, Sweden, Lithuania (2019 financial-sector campaign) [S5]
Chile, Mexico, Italy, China, South Korea, Taiwan (2019) [S6]
targeting.notes: Early operations were high-volume, largely untargeted spam via the Necurs botnet [S2][S3]; from 2018 targeting narrowed toward financial and retail organizations [S3][S4], and Fox-IT describes later ransomware victim selection as opportunistic [S7].

capabilities.summary: Large-scale malspam distribution of banking trojans and ransomware (Dridex, Locky, Jaff, GlobeImposter) [S2][S3]; macro-laden Office documents, HTML redirector attachments leading to Excel droppers, and URL-shortener lure links [S4][S5][S8]; custom and repurposed RATs and downloaders including ServHelper, FlawedGrace/GraceWire, FlawedAmmyy, Remote Manipulator System, Get2 and SDBbot (with application-shim persistence) [S4][S5][S6][S8]; Clop ransomware deployment across enterprise Windows servers with leak-site extortion [S7]; Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) exploitation using fake software updates, UAC bypass, wscript abuse and an MSBuild-compiled Mimikatz with Zerologon functionality [S9]; MirrorBlast and KiXtart loaders in 2021 [S12]. MITRE ATT&CK G0092 lists Cobalt Strike, TrickBot, Azorult, BloodHound and AdFind among associated software [S14].

campaigns.name: Proofpoint tracking begins
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint begins tracking TA505 high-volume spam campaigns.

campaigns.name: Dridex mass distribution
campaigns.summary: TA505 is behind many 2015 Dridex campaigns, briefly shifting to Shifu after law-enforcement disruption before returning to Dridex.

campaigns.name: Locky ransomware via Necurs
campaigns.summary: TA505 introduces Locky and, after July 2016, relies almost exclusively on it through year end.

campaigns.name: ServHelper and FlawedGrace campaigns
campaigns.summary: Malicious Word/Publisher documents deliver the new ServHelper backdoor, which drops FlawedGrace, against banks, retail and restaurants.

campaigns.name: FlawedAmmyy/RMS campaigns in Latin America and East Asia
campaigns.summary: Trend Micro reports targeting of Chile, Mexico, Italy, then China, South Korea and Taiwan with FlawedAmmyy or RMS.

campaigns.name: Get2 and SDBbot financial-sector campaign
campaigns.summary: Excel attachments drop Get2, which delivers SDBbot against financial institutions in Greece, Singapore, UAE and elsewhere, then US and Canadian targets.

campaigns.name: Maastricht University Clop ransomware
campaigns.summary: Fox-IT attributes the Clop deployment at Maastricht University to TA505.

campaigns.name: Dudear HTML redirector campaign
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports a shift to HTML redirector attachments leading to Excel files that install GraceWire.

campaigns.name: Zerologon exploitation (CHIMBORAZO)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft warns of fake software updates connecting to CHIMBORAZO infrastructure and exploiting Zerologon.

campaigns.name: Return of mass email campaigns
campaigns.summary: Proofpoint reports TA505 resuming mass emailing with FlawedGrace, KiXtart and MirrorBlast after a lull.

diamond.adversary: Financially motivated cybercrime actor tracked as Spandex Tempest/TA505/MONTY SPIDER [S1]; press reporting of Microsoft describes it as Russian [S9].
diamond.capability: Malspam with Office/HTML lures; ServHelper, FlawedGrace, FlawedAmmyy, Get2, SDBbot RATs; Clop ransomware; Zerologon exploitation [S4][S5][S7][S8][S9].
diamond.infrastructure: Necurs botnet for spam delivery [S2][S3]; actor C2 reached by fake update payloads [S9]; IP traceback services to log victims [S8]; Clop leak site [S7].
diamond.victim: Banks, financial, retail and restaurant organizations, universities and opportunistic enterprises across Europe, the Americas, the Middle East and Asia [S4][S5][S6][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Profit-driven extortion and fraud ecosystem; no state tasking identified in sources [S1][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise environments, Office macro execution, Active Directory domain controllers vulnerable to Zerologon [S4][S9].

gaps: Proofpoint, NCC Group/Fox-IT and CERT-FR primary documents could not be fetched (DNS failures); their content is cited from search-result summaries and secondary coverage.

Cluster boundaries: Microsoft tracks Lace Tempest (Clop affiliate; PaperCut, GoAnywhere, MOVEit-era activity) separately from Spandex Tempest, and Mandiant tracks FIN11 separately; 2021 Accellion and 2023 MOVEit/GoAnywhere activity is therefore not attributed to Spandex Tempest here [S11][S13].
Some press (e.g. coverage of Microsoft's 2020 posts) equates TA505 with Evil Corp; Microsoft's mapping does not support this and it is treated as a conflation [S1][S8].
No government attribution, indictment, or named individuals tied to TA505 were found in sources gathered.
Activity after 2021 that is specific to Spandex Tempest (as opposed to Lace Tempest/Clop) is not confirmed by Microsoft reporting found.
Aliases GRACEFUL SPIDER, GOLD TAHOE, Hive0065, SectorJ04 and ATK103 were not re-verified against vendor primary sources in this pass.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Email gateways, user workstations running Office, and Active Directory domain controllers are the relevant terrain, since the actor relies on malspam and has exploited Zerologon [S4][S9]. STEP 2: Rapid adoption of new exploits by a commodity actor signals near-term broad exploitation of disclosed flaws [S9]. STEP 3: Template is phishing (macro document or HTML redirector) to downloader (Get2/ServHelper), RAT (SDBbot/FlawedGrace), credential theft and domain compromise, then Clop deployment and leak-site extortion [S5][S7][S8]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic ransomware or extortion against installation-supporting contractors, universities or financial service providers. MDCOA is domain-wide encryption of mission-support networks via domain controller compromise. Candidate indicators: Excel/HTML attachments with macros, MSBuild or wscript launching unexpected code, application-shim persistence, Netlogon anomalies on DCs [S5][S8][S9].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track Microsoft, Proofpoint and CERT advisories naming TA505/Spandex Tempest and overlapping Clop clusters, keeping cluster names distinct [S1][S11][S13]. (2) Authorities: this is criminal activity, so response coordination runs through law enforcement and DC3 channels rather than military attribution of a state. (3) Mission assurance: prioritize patching of domain controllers and email hardening, since Zerologon and macro lures were key enablers [S9][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DIB and partner CERTs given the multinational victim set [S5][S6].
